title: Shingles Vaccine Linked to Lower Heart Attack and Stroke Risk, Major Studies Find
excerpt: A study published in Nature found the newer shingles vaccine reduced cardiovascular burden by 9% over seven years, adding to earlier research showing vaccinated heart patients were 46% less likely to suffer a serious cardiac event.
body:
• A study published August 26 in Nature found the Shingrix vaccine was associated with a 9% decrease in cardiovascular burden over seven years compared to an older vaccine, including lower risks of heart disease, heart failure, and atrial fibrillation.
  • A separate ACC study of nearly 247,000 U.S. adults with heart disease found vaccinated individuals were 46% less likely to suffer a major cardiac event and 66% less likely to die from any cause within a year.
  • Researchers say the cardiovascular protection from the shingles vaccine is comparable to the health benefit of quitting smoking.
  • The CDC recommends the shingles vaccine for all adults over 50; about one in three Americans will develop shingles in their lifetime.

The shingles vaccine may do far more than prevent a painful rash. Two major studies — one published this week in Nature and another presented at a leading cardiology conference earlier this year — have found that the vaccine is associated with significantly lower risks of heart attack, stroke, and cardiovascular death.

The findings carry particular relevance for Indian Americans and South Asians, who face disproportionately higher rates of cardiovascular disease compared to other ethnic groups in the United States.

The Nature Study: Seven Years of Data

In a study published August 26 in Nature, researchers from Oxford and Birmingham universities analyzed data from more than 70,000 U.S. adults aged 60 and over. They found that the newer recombinant shingles vaccine, Shingrix, was associated with a 9% decrease in overall cardiovascular burden over seven years compared to the older Zostavax vaccine.

The reduced risk extended to heart disease, heart failure, and atrial fibrillation — an irregular heart rhythm that can lead to blood clots and stroke. In men specifically, the newer vaccine was also linked to a decreased risk of stroke.

"Given the global burden of cardiovascular disease, these findings, if confirmed in clinical trials and mechanistic studies, would have important implications for public health."

Oxford and Birmingham research team, writing in Nature

The authors noted that preventing shingles infections may partly explain the cardiovascular benefit, given the established link between shingles and heart risk. But they suspect the vaccine may also induce immune and cellular changes that are independently cardioprotective. Further mechanistic research is needed to confirm the biological pathways.

ACC Study: Benefits Rival Quitting Smoking

The Nature findings build on a study presented in March at the American College of Cardiology's Annual Scientific Session in New Orleans. That research, led by Dr. Robert Nguyen at the University of California, Riverside, analyzed data from 246,822 U.S. adults with atherosclerotic heart disease — a condition caused by plaque buildup in arteries.

The results were striking. Within a year of vaccination, individuals who received the shingles vaccine were 46% less likely to experience a major adverse cardiac event, 32% less likely to suffer a heart attack, 25% less likely to have a stroke, and 66% less likely to die from any cause compared to unvaccinated patients.

"This vaccine has been found over and over again to have cardioprotective effects for reducing heart attack, stroke and death," Nguyen said. "Looking at the highest risk population, those with existing cardiovascular disease, these protective effects might be even greater than among the general public."

Nguyen said the level of cardiovascular protection from the shingles vaccine is comparable to the health benefit expected from quitting smoking.

Why It Matters

Shingles occurs when the varicella-zoster virus — the same virus that causes chickenpox — reactivates in the body, often decades after the initial infection. The CDC estimates that about one in three Americans will develop shingles in their lifetime. The two-dose Shingrix vaccine is about 90% effective in older adults and is recommended for everyone over age 50 and younger adults with weakened immune systems.

Previous research has shown that shingles infections can cause blood clots to form around the brain and heart, raising the risk of heart attacks and strokes. A 2025 European study found the vaccine's cardioprotective effects may last up to eight years, with the strongest benefits appearing two to three years after vaccination.

Both study teams cautioned that their findings show association, not causation, and noted limitations including potential healthy-user bias — people who get vaccinated may tend to have healthier behaviors overall. However, the large sample sizes and consistent results across multiple studies strengthen the evidence base.

The research also found a previous link between the shingles vaccine and lower dementia risk, suggesting the vaccine's benefits may extend beyond cardiovascular health.
